detail:
The National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) describes chronic low back pain management as centered on staying active, restoring function, and reducing pain rather than prolonged bed rest. Sources describe physical therapy as a common part of care plans: therapists typically build programs around core and back strengthening, flexibility, posture and body mechanics, and a gradual return to regular activity, with aerobic activity often included as tolerated.

NIAMS notes that clinicians may discuss medicine classes such as analgesics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), along with heat or cold applications, as part of a broader plan, and that some care plans include behavioral approaches that address sleep, stress, and fear of movement. Invasive procedures and surgery are generally described as options clinicians consider only for specific structural causes or persistent, disabling symptoms after conservative care, not as routine treatment for chronic low back pain without a clear target.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing chronic low back pain.
sourceName: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
summary: NIAMS describes chronic low back pain management centered on staying active and physical therapy to restore function, with medicine classes and behavioral approaches as parts of some care plans and surgery reserved for specific causes.
takeaways: staying active and restoring function are central goals sources describe
therapists typically build programs around strengthening and flexibility
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Chronic Low Back Pain: managing persistent pain day to day
